```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using MatrixCommunityModels
using ResilienceCore
using LinearAlgebra, Printf, Statistics
using Plots
```

## Matrix communities in ResilienceCore's terms

[ResilienceCore.jl](https://github.com/ecorecipes/ResilienceCore.jl) computes stability and
resilience metrics that dispatch on what a matrix *means*: the Jacobian at a fixed point, a
density-independent projection matrix, a periodic model. This package hands it three kinds of
object:

- `linearise(c, n, env)`: the Jacobian of one step of a closed community at a fixed point
  `n`, as a `DiscreteJacobian`. With `period = k` it is the Jacobian of `k` steps at a point
  of a `k`-cycle.
- `periodic_operator(invader, pool, envs)`: the matrices of a rare invader over a cycle of
  environments, as a `PeriodicOperator`.
- `MCMState(c, n, env)`: a community at a fixed point with ResilienceCore's community
  interface, so that its simulated press, removal and extinction experiments run unchanged.

For a discrete-time fixed point, ResilienceCore's metrics are:

- `isstable`: whether every eigenvalue of `J` has modulus below one;
- `resilience`: `-ln ρ(J)`, the rate at which small perturbations die out per step;
- `reactivity`: `ln ‖J‖₂`, positive when some perturbation grows in the first step;
- `max_amplification`: the largest growth of any perturbation before it decays, and when.

## One beetle: a stable equilibrium that amplifies

The larva-pupa-adult (LPA) beetle of [vignette 21](../21_flour_beetles/21_flour_beetles.md),
alone, with the rates of `TRIBOLIUM_EDMUNDS_2003`. The state is `[L, P, A]`, in two-week
steps.

```{julia}
beetle(; mu_a = 0.02, cpa = 0.012 / 0.4) =
    flour_beetle(:castaneum; b = 10, mu_l = 0.2, mu_a = mu_a,
                 eats = [:castaneum => (larvae_eggs = 0.01 / 0.4, adults_eggs = 0.01 / 0.4, adults_pupae = cpa)])
one = beetle()
e = periodic_point(one, [30.0, 30, 100], nothing)
J = linearise(one, e.n, nothing)
(state = round.(e.n; digits = 1), stable = isstable(J), resilience = resilience(J),
 reactivity = reactivity(J), max_amplification = max_amplification(J))
```

The equilibrium is stable, but perturbations die out slowly (a resilience of
`{julia} round(resilience(J); digits = 3)` per step, so a perturbation takes about
`{julia} round(Int, log(10) / resilience(J))` steps to shrink tenfold), and the
equilibrium is reactive: the worst perturbation grows by a factor of
`{julia} round(max_amplification(J)[1]; digits = 1)` over the first
`{julia} max_amplification(J)[2] == 1 ? "step" : "$(max_amplification(J)[2]) steps"` before it
decays.

## Raising adult mortality: cycles and chaos

Costantino et al. (1997) set adult mortality at 96% per two weeks in laboratory cultures and
varied the rate at which adults eat pupae, `c_pa`, taking the LPA model through cycles and
chaos. The same design with the rates above (illustrative; they are not the fitted values of
that experiment):

```{julia}
cpas = 0:0.005:1
attractor = map(cpas) do cpa
    c, x = beetle(mu_a = 0.96, cpa = cpa), [100.0, 100, 100]
    for _ in 1:500
        x = advance(c, x, nothing)
    end
    out = Float64[]
    for _ in 1:100
        x = advance(c, x, nothing)
        push!(out, x[1])
    end
    out
end
ρ = map(cpas) do cpa
    c = beetle(mu_a = 0.96, cpa = cpa)
    p = periodic_point(c, [50.0, 40, 30], nothing)
    maximum(abs, eigvals(operator(linearise(c, p.n, nothing))))
end
p1 = scatter(repeat(collect(cpas); inner = 100), reduce(vcat, attractor); ms = 0.8, msw = 0, color = :black,
             legend = false, ylabel = "larvae on the attractor", title = "μa = 0.96")
p2 = plot(cpas, ρ; lw = 2, legend = false, xlabel = "c_pa (adults eating pupae)",
          ylabel = "ρ(J) at the equilibrium")
hline!(p2, [1]; ls = :dash, color = :gray)
plot(p1, p2; layout = (2, 1), size = (700, 550))
```

The equilibrium is unstable at every `c_pa` (`ρ(J) > 1`, `resilience < 0`): with this many
adults dying, the population never settles. What it does instead depends on `c_pa`: a
two-cycle without cannibalism of pupae, irregular dynamics at low rates, then an eight-cycle
and, at the highest rates, a three-cycle.

A cycle is analysed in the same way, with the Jacobian of one pass around it. Its
eigenvalues are the cycle's multipliers (those of `periodic_point`), and its resilience per
step is that of the period map divided by the period:

```{julia}
function cycle(cpa, k)
    c, x = beetle(mu_a = 0.96, cpa = cpa), [100.0, 100, 100]
    for _ in 1:600
        x = advance(c, x, nothing)
    end
    p = periodic_point(c, x, nothing; period = k)
    Jk = linearise(c, p.n, nothing; period = k)
    return (c_pa = cpa, period = k, converged = p.converged, stable = isstable(Jk),
            resilience_per_step = resilience(Jk) / k)
end
[cycle(0.0, 2), cycle(0.5, 8), cycle(1.0, 3)]
```

All three cycles are stable, each settling at a rate comparable to the stable equilibrium of
the long-lived beetle above.

## Two beetles: presses and removals

`MCMState` gives a community the interface that ResilienceCore's simulated experiments use.
Pressing a species multiplies the mortality hazard of every one of its stages: a stage that
survives a step with probability `σ` survives with probability `σ^f`. Removing a species
holds its stages at zero. After each perturbation the community returns to a fixed point.

The two-species model of Edmunds et al. (2003) has a stable coexistence equilibrium when
larvae eat a moderate share of the other species' eggs (region A of that paper):

```{julia}
two = flour_beetle_competition(merge(TRIBOLIUM_EDMUNDS_2003, (c_el = [0.01 0.018; 0.018 0.01],)))
s = MCMState(two, periodic_point(two, [8.0, 6, 34, 21, 17, 69], nothing).n, nothing)
(species = species_names(two), abundance = round.(state(s); digits = 1), stable = isstable(linearise(s)),
 local_tolerance = local_mortality_tolerances(s), global_tolerance = global_mortality_tolerance(s))
```

`local_mortality_tolerances` is the smallest increase in one species' mortality, in steps of
10%, that loses any species; `global_mortality_tolerance` the smallest multiplier of every
species' mortality that does. *T. confusum* is lost when its own mortality rises by
`{julia} round(Int, 100local_mortality_tolerances(s)[1])`%, yet no species is lost until the
mortality of both rises `{julia} round(global_mortality_tolerance(s); digits = 1)`-fold: a
press on one species alone tips the competition, a press on both does not. Removing either
species releases the other:

```{julia}
[(removed = species_names(two)[i], left = round.(state(without_species(s, i)); digits = 1))
 for i in present_species(s)]
```

## Riparian guilds in a constant flood regime

The five riparian guilds of [vignette 3](../03_riparian_guilds/03_riparian_guilds.md)
compete for free space, and floods and droughts kill stage-specific fractions of each. The
experiments need a fixed point, so each kind of year is held constant here, which removes the
fluctuations the guilds normally live with:

```{julia}
rip = riparian_model(corrected = true)
flood_year = first(e for e in rip.envs if e.flood == 1)
dry_year = first(e for e in rip.envs if e.flood == 0 && e.drought == 0)
wet = MCMState(rip.community, rip.n0, flood_year)
dry = MCMState(rip.community, rip.n0, dry_year)
(flood_every_year = wet, no_floods = dry)
```

Without floods, sagebrush (`S`) excludes every other guild. With a flood every year sagebrush
is lost and the other four persist at a stable equilibrium. (The authors' script kept at least
10 sagebrush in each stage, which held it in; the corrected model has no such floor, see
vignette 3.)

```{julia}
guilds = species_names(rip.community)
alive = present_species(wet)
(abundance = round.(state(wet); sigdigits = 3), largest_multiplier = maximum(abs, eigvals(operator(linearise(wet)))),
 local_tolerance = guilds[alive] .=> local_mortality_tolerances(wet))
```

Cottonwood (`C`) is the most sensitive to extra mortality of its own. Removing one guild at a
time shows who takes the space (abundances of the four guilds present, relative to before):

```{julia}
change(t) = guilds[alive] .=> round.(state(t)[alive] ./ state(wet)[alive]; digits = 2)
removals = [(removed = guilds[i], abundance_relative_to_before = change(without_species(wet, i)))
            for i in present_species(wet)]
removals
```

Removing willow (`W`) multiplies cottonwood, tamarisk and meadow by the same factor, about
`{julia} round(Int, state(without_species(wet, 3))[1] / state(wet)[1])`: every guild's
recruitment is proportional to the same free space, so freeing space scales them alike.
Removing any other guild changes the rest by about 1% or less.

## Two kinds of press

What "raising mortality" means is a modelling choice, and `MCMState` offers two:

- `press = :hazard` (the default) multiplies each stage's mortality hazard by `f`, so a stage
  that survives a step with probability `σ` survives with probability `σ^f`;
- `press = :removal` removes a fraction `m = removal_scale × (f - 1)` of every stage after
  each step, as harvesting or culling would. It is an added loss, not the baseline mortality
  multiplied by `f`.

Both leave the model unchanged at `f = 1`, and they differ most where survival is far from
one. Cottonwood seedlings almost all die in their first year:

```{julia}
σ = vec(sum(matrix_model(rip.community, :C, wet.n, flood_year).U; dims = 1))
f = 1.1
[(stage = k, survival = round(σ[k]; sigdigits = 2), kept_hazard = round(σ[k]^(f - 1); digits = 3),
  kept_removal = round(1 - (f - 1); digits = 3)) for k in eachindex(σ)]
```

A 10% hazard press halves the survival of seedlings and barely touches mature trees; a 10%
removal takes the same share of every stage. Pressing cottonwood alone, at the same `f`:

```{julia}
wet_removal = MCMState(rip.community, rip.n0, flood_year; press = :removal)
press_C = [f, 1, 1, 1, 1]
(hazard = guilds[alive] .=> round.(state(with_mortality(wet, press_C))[alive] ./ state(wet)[alive]; digits = 3),
 removal = guilds[alive] .=> round.(state(with_mortality(wet_removal, press_C))[alive] ./ state(wet_removal)[alive]; digits = 3),
 tolerance_hazard = local_mortality_tolerances(wet)[1],
 tolerance_removal = local_mortality_tolerances(wet_removal)[1])
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
hz = state(with_mortality(wet, press_C)) ./ state(wet)
rm = state(with_mortality(wet_removal, press_C)) ./ state(wet_removal)
pct(x) = round(100 * abs(x - 1); digits = 1);
```

Under the hazard press cottonwood does not decline at all: it rises by
`{julia} pct(hz[1])`%, like the other guilds. The extra deaths fall mostly on seedlings, and the
space they free is recruited into by every guild, cottonwood included. Under the removal
press cottonwood falls by `{julia} pct(rm[1])`% while the others rise. Cottonwood is lost at a
`{julia} round(Int, 100local_mortality_tolerances(wet)[1])`% hazard press but at a
`{julia} round(Int, 100local_mortality_tolerances(wet_removal)[1])`% removal press. Which press
is right depends on the perturbation being modelled: a harsher flood or drought acts on
survival, harvesting or browsing removes a share of what stands.

## With EcologicalResilience.jl

`jacobian` and `linearise` are ResilienceCore's functions, so this package and others built
on ResilienceCore (EcologicalResilience.jl, FoodWebDynamics.jl) share them. EcologicalResilience
also exports its own `equilibrium` and `subcommunity`; when both packages are loaded, write
`MatrixCommunityModels.equilibrium`. Since version 0.2.0 this package is on the SciMLBase 3
line, as EcologicalResilience.jl is, so the two can be installed in one environment.

## References

Costantino, R. F., Desharnais, R. A., Cushing, J. M. & Dennis, B. (1997). Chaotic dynamics in
an insect population. *Science* 275, 389-391.

Edmunds, J., Cushing, J. M., Costantino, R. F., Henson, S. M., Dennis, B. & Desharnais,
R. A. (2003). Park's *Tribolium* competition experiments: a non-equilibrium species
coexistence hypothesis. *Journal of Animal Ecology* 72, 703-712.

Lytle, D. A., Merritt, D. M., Tonkin, J. D., Olden, J. D. & Reynolds, L. V. (2017).
Linking river flow regimes to riparian plant guilds: a community-wide modeling approach.
*Ecological Applications* 27, 1338-1350.
